Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 57, verse 1–3:

(p-468) Surat al-Hadid

It is Medinan according to the majority of scholars; al-Kalbi said it is Meccan.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah﴾. In this glorification (tasbih, the act of declaring God free from imperfection) there are three interpretations:

First: it means that the creation of what is in the heavens and the earth necessitates His transcendence above likenesses and resemblances.

Second: the glorification of Allah by speech, free of what the atheists (al-mulhidun) attribute to Him, and this is the view of the majority.

Third: that it refers to prayer (salah), which is called tasbih because it includes tasbih. This was said by Sufyan and al-Dahhak.

So His saying ﴿Whatever is in the heavens glorifies Allah﴾ means the angels and whatever else is in them, and ﴿whatever is in the earth﴾ means the animals and the inanimate. We have already mentioned the glorification and prostration of inanimate things in a way that suffices without repetition.

﴿And He is the Mighty﴾ in His victory, ﴿the Wise﴾ in His governance.

(p-469) ﴿He is the First and the Last﴾. By "the First" he means that He is before everything by His eternity, and by "the Last" that He is after everything by His permanence.

﴿And the Manifest and the Hidden﴾. In this there are three interpretations:

First: the Manifest is above everything by His exaltedness, and the Hidden is His encompassing of everything by His nearness. This was said by Ibn Hayyan.

Second: that He is the Subduer of what is apparent and hidden, as the Exalted said, ﴿So We supported those who believed against their enemy, and they became the victorious (zahirin)﴾.

Third: the Knower of what is apparent and what is hidden.

﴿And He is, of everything, Knowing﴾, meaning of the First, the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden.

For the people of insight (ashab al-khawatir) regarding this there are three views:

First: the First in beginning His favors, the Last in concluding them with beneficence, the Manifest in displaying His proofs to minds, and the Hidden in His knowledge of the inner matters.

Second: the First by unveiling the conditions of the Hereafter when you desire it, the Last by unveiling the conditions of this world when you renounce it, the Manifest upon the hearts of His friends when they recognize Him, and the Hidden upon the hearts of His enemies when they deny Him.

Third: the First before every known thing, the Last after every sealed thing, the Manifest above every inscribed thing, and the Hidden encompassing every concealed thing.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 57, verses 4–6:

﴿And what comes out of it﴾. Muqatil said: "From plants and from other than plants."

﴿And what descends from the sky and what ascends into it﴾. Muqatil said: "From the angels." Others said: "From angels and from other than angels."

It may also bear another meaning: what enters the earth of seed, and what comes out of it of crops, and what descends from the sky of decree, and what ascends into it of deeds, so that they may know the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of them in what they reveal or conceal, and the efficacy of His decree over them whether they desire it or dislike it.

﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾. In this there are two interpretations:

The first: His knowledge is with you wherever you are, such that nothing of your deeds is hidden from Him. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: His power is with you wherever you are, such that nothing of your affairs can overpower Him.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on surah 57, verses 7–12:

﴿And spend of that in which He has made you successors.﴾ This spending may bear two meanings:

First: that it is the obligatory zakat.

Second: that it is other forms of obedience besides zakat.

Regarding ﴿of that in which He has made you successors﴾ there are two views:

First: it means of that in which He has made you to live long by means of provision. This is the view of Mujahid.

Second: of that in which He has made you successors by your inheriting it from those before you. This is the view of al-Hasan.

A third possibility is: of that in which He has made you successors in the duty of discharging its rights.

﴿And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth.﴾ This may bear two meanings:

First: its meaning is that sovereignty over the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah.

Second: that the two return to Him when those upon them pass away, as an inheritance returns to its rightful heir.

﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest.﴾ Concerning this there are two views:

First: not equal are those who embraced Islam before the conquest of Makkah and fought, and those who embraced Islam after its conquest and fought. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

Second: it means those who spent their wealth in jihad and fought. This is the view of Qatadah.

Regarding this "conquest" there are two views:

First: the conquest of Makkah. This is the view of Zayd ibn Aslam.

Second: the conquest of Hudaybiyyah. This is the view of al-Sha'bi. Qatadah said: There were two kinds of fighting, one of which is superior to the other, and there were two kinds of spending, one of which is superior to the other. Fighting and spending before the conquest of Makkah were superior to fighting and spending after it.

﴿And to each Allah has promised the best.﴾ Concerning this there are two views:

First: that "the best" (al-husna) is the good reward. This is the view of Muqatil.

Second: it is Paradise. This is the view of Mujahid.

A third possibility is that al-husna is acceptance and recompense.

(p-472) ﴿Who is it that would lend Allah a goodly loan?﴾ Concerning this there are five sayings:

The first: the goodly loan is that one says: "Subhan Allah, al-hamdu lillah, la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah, Allahu akbar." This was related by Sufyan from Ibn Hayyan.

The second: it is spending on one's family. This is the view of Zayd ibn Aslam.

The third: it is voluntary acts of worship. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The fourth: it is doing good deeds. The Arabs say: "I have with so-and-so a loan of truthfulness (qard sidq) or a loan of evil (qard su')," when he has done good or evil to him. From this is the saying of the poet:

"And she repays with greetings for the loan she advanced, for what their hands had done and what slipped."

The fifth: it is spending in the way of Allah. This is the view of Muqatil ibn Hayyan.

Regarding His words ﴿goodly﴾ there are two meanings:

First: that his soul is content with it. This is the view of Muqatil.

Second: seeking reward for it from Allah. This is the view of al-Kalbi. It was called a loan because of the deserving of its reward. This is what Labid said:

"And when you are repaid with a loan, then repay it; indeed a young man repays, not a camel."

Regarding calling it ﴿goodly﴾ there are two meanings:

First: because it is spent on good purposes.

Second: because there is no reminder of favour in it and no harm.

﴿That He may multiply it for him.﴾ Concerning this there are two meanings:

First: He multiplies the loan, because the reward of a good deed is ten times its like.

Second: He multiplies the reward, bestowing favour without limit.

﴿And he will have a noble reward.﴾ Concerning this there are four meanings:

First: he did not humble himself in seeking it.

Second: because its worth is noble.

Third: because its giver is noble.

When Abu al-Dahdah heard it, he gave a garden in charity, and he was the first to give charity after this verse.

(p-473) Sa'id ibn Jubayr related that: "The Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ when this verse was revealed and said: 'O Muhammad, is your Lord poor, asking His servants for a loan?' So Allah revealed: ﴿Certainly Allah has heard the statement of those who said, 'Indeed, Allah is poor'﴾ [3:181]."

﴿On the Day you will see the believing men and believing women, their light running before them and on their right.﴾ Concerning their light there are three meanings:

First: it is a radiance Allah gives them as reward and honour. This is the meaning of Qatadah's view.

Second: it is the guidance which He decreed for them. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Third: it is the light of their deeds and obedience.

Ibn Mas'ud said: Their light is according to the measure of their deeds. They pass over the Sirat, and among them is one whose light is like a palm tree, and the least of them in light is one whose light is on the big toe of his foot, which is kindled at times and extinguished at others.

Al-Dahhak said: No one is given light on the Day of Resurrection. When they reach the Sirat, the light of the hypocrites is extinguished. When the believers saw that, they feared that their light would be extinguished as the light of the hypocrites had been, so they said: ﴿Our Lord, perfect for us our light﴾ [66:8]. Concerning His words ﴿before them﴾ there are two meanings:

First: that they may be illuminated by it upon the Sirat. This is the view of al-Hasan.

Second: that it may be for them a guide to Paradise. This is the view of Muqatil.

Concerning His words "on their right" it refers to charities, zakat and paths of goodness.

Fourth: "by their faith" in this world and their belief in the recompense. This is the view of Muqatil.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Good tidings for you today: gardens﴾ bear two meanings: (p-474) First: that their light is their good tidings of the gardens.

Second: that it is good tidings from the angels, whom they meet with them on the Day of Resurrection. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

؎ O Abu Hind, do not hasten against us, and wait for us; we will inform you of certainty.

﴿It will be said: Return behind you and seek a light.﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: return to the place from which we took the light and seek light from there.

The second: return and do deeds by which Allah will place a light before you.

The first: that the believers say it to them.
The second: that the angels say it to them.

The first: the deceptions of Satan. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: the worldly life. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: "We will be forgiven." This was said by Abu Sinan.

The second: their being cast into the Fire. This was said by Qatadah.

The first: Satan. This was said by Ikrimah.

The second: the world. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 57, verses 16–17:

The first view: they were revealed concerning the people of Musa (peace be upon him) before the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent. This was said by Ibn Hayyan.

The second view: they concern the hypocrites who professed faith with their tongues and disbelieved in their hearts. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The third view: they concern the believers of our community. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, and al-Qasim ibn Muhammad.

Then scholars differed about them in three statements:

The first: what Abu Hazim narrated from 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The time between our accepting Islam and being rebuked with this verse was only four years, so some of us began looking at one another, saying, 'What have we innovated?'"

al-Hasan said: "He (Allah) was slow to (rebuke) them, though they were the most beloved of His creation to Him."

The second: what Qatadah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that Allah was slow regarding the hearts of the emigrants, so He rebuked them at the end of thirteen years, and He said, "Has the time not come for those who believe..." (the verse).

The third: what al-Mas'udi narrated from al-Qasim, who said: "The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) once grew weary and said, 'O Messenger of Allah, relate to us,' so Allah revealed, 'We relate to you the best of stories.' Then they grew weary again and said, 'Relate to us, O Messenger of Allah,' so Allah revealed, 'Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should be humbled (khushu') at the remembrance of Allah?'"

Shaddad ibn Aws said: "It used to be narrated to us from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: 'The first thing to be removed from people is khushu''."

Has the time not come for me, O heart, to abandon ignorance,
and for the clear white hair to bring me understanding?

The third: that their hearts should be distressed out of fear of Allah.

Regarding "the remembrance of Allah" here, there are two possibilities:

The first: that it is the Qur'an, said by Muqatil.

The second: that it is the rights of Allah, and this is a possibility.

Regarding ﴿and what has been revealed of the truth﴾, there are three aspects:

The first: the Qur'an, said by Muqatil.

The second: the lawful and the unlawful, said by al-Kalbi.

The third: it may be what He revealed of the clear signs and guidance.

Regarding ﴿Know that Allah gives life to the earth after its death﴾, there are three aspects:

The first: He softens hearts after their hardness, said by Salih al-Muri.

The second: it may mean that He corrects corruption.

The third: that it is a parable He set forth for the revival of the dead.

﴿Indeed, the men who give charity and the women who give charity﴾ (al-muṣṣaddiqīn wal-muṣṣaddiqāt) has two interpretations:

First: those who affirm (muṣaddiqīn) Allah and His Messenger.

Second: those who give charity (mutaṣaddiqīn) with their wealth in obedience to Allah.

﴿And those who believed in Allah and His messengers—they are the ṣiddīqūn (the truthful ones)﴾, meaning: the believers, through their affirmation of Allah and His messengers.

﴿And the martyrs, with their Lord, they will have their reward and their light﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

First: that those who believed in Allah and His messengers are the ṣiddīqūn, and they are also the martyrs with their Lord. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

Second: that His statement ﴿They are the ṣiddīqūn﴾ is a complete sentence. And His statement ﴿And the martyrs with their Lord﴾ is a new (independent) sentence. Concerning who they are there are two opinions:

First: that they are the messengers, who bear witness over their nations concerning their affirmation and denial. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Second: that they are the nations of the messengers, who bear witness on the Day of Resurrection.

Concerning what they bear witness to, there are two opinions:

First: they bear witness against themselves regarding what they did of obedience and disobedience. This is the meaning of the statement of Mujahid.

Second: they bear witness on behalf of their prophets concerning the conveyance of the message to their nations. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Muqatil stated a third opinion: that they are those killed in the way of Allah; ﴿for them is their reward with their Lord﴾, meaning the reward of their deeds.

﴿And their light﴾ has two interpretations:

First: their light over the Sirat (bridge).

Second: their faith in the world, related by al-Kalbi.(p-480)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 57, verses 20–21:

﴿Know that the life of this world is only play and amusement﴾ Concerning this there are two interpretations:

First: It is eating and drinking. This is the view of Qatadah.

Second: It is according to what is known from its name (la'b, play; lahw, amusement). Mujahid said: every play is amusement.

It may also bear a third interpretation: that play is what makes one desire the world, and amusement is what diverts one from the Hereafter.

It may also bear a fourth: that play is acquiring possessions, and amusement is women.

﴿and adornment﴾ may bear two interpretations:

First: that the world is a fleeting adornment.

Second: that it is everything that one engages with in the world for other than obedience.

﴿and boasting among yourselves﴾ may bear two interpretations:

First: by physical stature and strength.

Second: by lineage, according to the custom of the Arabs in competing through their forefathers.

﴿and rivalry in wealth and children﴾ because the custom of the Jahiliyyah was to vie in wealth and children, whereas the believers vie in faith and acts of obedience.

Then He struck for them a parable of vegetation: ﴿like the example of a rain whose vegetation pleases the disbelievers; then it dries up﴾ after greenness.

﴿So you see it turned yellow; then it becomes debris﴾ by the crushing winds, so it perishes after its beauty. Likewise is the world of the disbeliever.

﴿Race to forgiveness from your Lord﴾ Concerning this there are four interpretations: (p-481)
First: the Prophet ﷺ. This is the view of Abu Sa'id.

Second: the first row (of prayer). This is the view of Rabah ibn 'Ubayd.

Third: the first takbir with the imam. This is the view of Makhul.

Fourth: repentance. This is the view of al-Kalbi.

﴿and a Garden whose width is like the width of the heaven﴾ as an encouragement toward its vastness. He mentioned only the width, not the length, because the width indicates the length, and because it is the custom of the Arabs to express the vastness of a thing by its width rather than its length. The poet said:

"As if the lands of God, though wide, upon the fearful, pursued one, were a ring's circle."

﴿That is the bounty of God; He gives it to whom He wills.﴾ Concerning this there are two interpretations:

First: it is Paradise. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Second: it is religion. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

Concerning ﴿whom He wills﴾ there are two opinions:

First: from among the believers, if the bounty is said to be Paradise.

Second: from among all creation, if it is said to be religion.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 57, verses 22–24:

﴿No affliction befalls in the earth﴾ — there are two views concerning it:

First: calamities in the crops and fruits.

Second: drought and high prices.

﴿Nor in yourselves﴾ — there are four views concerning it:

First: in one's religion; this is said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

(p-482) Second: illnesses and ailments; this is said by Qatadah.

Third: the carrying out of the prescribed punishments (hudud); this is said by Ibn Hibban.

Fourth: straitened livelihood; this is the meaning of the narration of Ibn Jurayj.

﴿Except in a Book﴾ — meaning the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

﴿Before We bring it into being﴾ — Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: before We create the calamities and decree them.

﴿So that you do not despair over what has escaped you﴾ — concerning it there are two views:

First: of the provision that was not decreed for you; this is said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak.

Second: of well-being and abundance that was not decreed for you; this is said by Ibn Jubayr.

﴿And do not exult in what He has given you﴾ — concerning it there are two views:

First: of the worldly things; this is said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: of well-being and abundance; this is the implication of the saying of Ibn Jubayr.

ʿIkrimah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿so that you do not despair over what has escaped you and do not exult in what He has given you﴾, that he said: No one is free of sorrow and joy, but the believer makes his affliction patience (sabr) and his good fortune gratitude (shukr).

﴿Those who are miserly and enjoin people to be miserly﴾ — concerning it there are five interpretations:

First: "Those who are miserly" means miserly with knowledge, and "enjoin people to be miserly" means they forbid people from teaching anything; this is said by Ibn Jubayr.

Second: that they are the Jews, who were miserly with what was in the Torah concerning the mention of Muhammad (ﷺ); this is said by al-Kalbi and al-Suddi.

Third: that it is miserliness in paying God's right from their wealth; this is said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

Fourth: that it is miserliness in giving charity and the rights due; this is said by ʿAmir ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Ashʿari.

Fifth: that it is miserliness with what is in their hands; this is said by Tawus.

The scholars of the "khawatir" (the study of inner impulses and thoughts) distinguished between the miser and the generous person in two ways:

First: that the miser is one who takes pleasure in withholding, and the generous one is one who takes pleasure in giving.

(p-483) Second: that the miser gives only when asked, and the generous one gives without being asked.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 57, verse 25:**

﴿And We sent down iron﴾. On this there are two opinions:

One: that God sent it down with Adam.

ʿIkrima narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Three things descended with Adam: the Black Stone, which was whiter than snow; the staff of Moses, which was of myrtle (ās) from Paradise, ten cubits long, the same height as Moses; and iron. Three things were sent down with iron: the anvil (al-sindān), the tongs (al-kalbatān), and the hammer (al-mīqaʿa), which is the mihraqa (hammer)."

The second: that it is from the earth and was not sent down from the sky. In that case, the meaning of His words ﴿And We sent down﴾ is understood in one of two ways:

One: that is, We made it manifest (aẓharnāhu).

The second: because its origin is from the water sent down from the sky, so its substance coalesces in the earth until, through smelting, it becomes iron.

﴿In it is great might﴾. On this there are two interpretations:

One: because by its weapons and implements war takes place, which is great might.

The second: because in it there is intense fear of being killed.

﴿And benefits for mankind﴾. This may have two meanings:

One: what the iron coats of mail (durūʿ al-ḥadīd) ward off from them of harm, and what bring them to war and victory.

The second: what is held back from them of hardship through fear of it.

Qutrub said: "The might (al-baʾs) is the weapons (al-silāḥ), and the benefit (al-manfaʿa) is the implements (al-āla)."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 57, verses 26–27:

﴿And We placed in the hearts of those who followed him compassion (ra'fah) and mercy (rahmah)﴾ This may bear two meanings:

First: ra'fah is gentleness, and rahmah is tenderness of care.

Second: ra'fah is the lightening of burdens (takhfif al-kall), and rahmah is the bearing of hardship (tahammul al-thiql).

﴿But monasticism (rahbaniyyah) they invented﴾ Concerning this there are two readings. The first, with a fatha on the rā', means fear (al-khawf) arising from dread (al-rahb).

The second, with a ḍammah on the rā', is attributed to monks (al-ruhban), and its meaning is that they invented a monasticism which they themselves initiated.

The cause of this, as related by al-Ḍaḥḥāk: after ʿĪsā, they committed the forbidden acts for three hundred years, and those who remained upon the method of ʿĪsā denounced this to them, so they killed them. Then a group who remained after them said: "If we forbid them, they will kill us, so there is no room for us to remain among them." So they withdrew from women and took up hermitages (ṣawāmiʿ). This is what they invented of monasticism, which none before them had done, though they were doers of good in it.

﴿We did not prescribe it for them﴾ meaning it was not prescribed for them. Concerning this there are three interpretations:

First: it is the abandonment of women and the taking of hermitages; this is said by Qatadah.

Second: it is their joining the mountains and their dwelling in deserts; a marfūʿ report has been related concerning this.

Third: it is the cutting off from people and the solitary devotion to worship.

(p-485) Concerning the ra'fah and rahmah which He placed in their hearts there are two interpretations:

[The first]: that He placed them in their hearts by commanding them to them and encouraging them toward them.

The second: He placed them by creating them within them, and they were praised for their alluding to them.

﴿We did not prescribe it for them, except in seeking the pleasure of God﴾ meaning it was not prescribed for them before they invented it, nor was it prescribed for them afterward.

Second: that they voluntarily undertook it through their invention, and then it was prescribed for them afterward; this is said by al-Ḥasan.

﴿But they did not observe it with its proper observance﴾ Concerning this there are two interpretations:

First: that they did not observe it because of their denial of Muḥammad.

Second: by altering their religion and changing it before the mission of the Messenger (ﷺ); this is said by ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 57, verse 28–29:

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger﴾. Its meaning is: O you who have believed in Moses and Jesus, believe in Muhammad.

﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾. In this there are two views:

The first: one of the two rewards is for their belief in the prophets who came before, and the other is for their belief in Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: one of them is the reward of this world, and the other is the reward of the Hereafter. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

It may also carry a third meaning: one of them is the reward for abstaining from sins, and the second is the reward for performing acts of obedience.

It may also carry a fourth meaning: one of them is the reward for upholding the rights of Allah, and the second is the reward for upholding the rights of the servants.

﴿And He will make for you a light by which you will walk﴾. In this there are two views:

The first: it is the Qur'an. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: it is guidance. This was said by Mujahid.

It may also carry a third meaning: it is the religion that is followed for the benefit of this world and the reward of the Hereafter.

Abu Burda ibn Abi Musa al-Ashʿari narrated from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three people will be given their reward twice: a man who believed in the first Book and the last Book; a man who had a slave-girl, educated her well, treated her education well, then freed her and married her; and a servant who worshipped his Lord well and gave sincere counsel to his master."

﴿So that the People of the Book may know﴾. Al-Akhfash said: its meaning is "so that the People of the Book may know," and "lā" is an extra, superfluous particle. Al-Farra' said: it means "so that the People of the Book may not know," and "lā" is an extra particle in a sentence that is preceded by a negation.

﴿that they have no power over anything of the bounty of Allah﴾. In this there are two views:

The first: of the religion of Allah, which is Islam. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: of the provision of Allah. This was said by al-Kalbi.

There is also a third view: that the bounty refers to the favours of Allah which cannot be counted.
